Thursday night: Vikas changed a line, ran the program, changed another, ran it, until two in the morning. It crashed differently each time, and he lost track of what he had edited.

Friday: Sunaina, his lab partner, looked at the screen and asked, 'What did you change since it last worked?' He couldn't say. He opened a notebook and wrote three column headings: Attempt, Change, Result. Then he restored the last working copy.

Saturday: Change one, rename a variable, result: same. Change two, swap the loop order, result: crash moves earlier. Change three, print the list length before the loop, result: zero. The file reader was failing quietly. He fixed the file path and the program ran. It had taken twenty minutes.

qa.q: How long did it take to find the fault once Vikas kept the log?
How did Vikas feel at two in the morning after losing track of his edits?
qa.a: Vikas felt frustrated and confused, since the program crashed differently each time and he could not tell why.

qa.q: What other approach could Vikas use to track his changes?
qa.a: Vikas could save each change as a small step in a version-control tool, since it records what changed and allows going back.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have seen the first night of random edits?
qa.a: Sunaina probably saw guesswork that was hard to trace, which is why Sunaina asked what had changed since it last worked.

grounding: Shows a student who, after a night of random edits, starts noting each change and its result and finds the fault within twenty minutes.

Ishita, beta, you think I was always organised? Let your Lokesh Mama tell you about third year.
I had a C program for the data structures lab that crashed on the fourth test case. I sat up all night making random edits. Change a loop. Run. Change a pointer. Run. By four in the morning I had changed so much I could not remember what the code looked like at midnight.
Then my roommate woke up, looked at my screen and said, "Write down what you change. One line each time."
I was too tired to argue. So I opened a notebook. Change: array size to 101. Result: still crashes. Change: loop ends at n minus one. Result: passes.
Twenty minutes, Ishita. One night of chaos and then twenty minutes with a notebook. I still keep that habit.

qa.q: What was the change that finally made the program pass?
qa.a: The change was making the loop end at n minus one.

qa.q: How was Lokesh feeling by four in the morning?
qa.a: Lokesh was exhausted and lost, having changed so much he couldn't remember what the code looked like at midnight.

qa.q: When the roommate suggested a log, what other choice could Lokesh have made, and what would likely have happened?
qa.a: He could have kept editing at random out of tiredness, and he would probably still have been stuck at dawn.

qa.q: How might the roommate have seen Lokesh that night?
qa.a: The roommate probably saw a friend going in circles and offered one simple habit that changed the whole night.

grounding: It shows a student who switches from random edits to noting each change and its result, and finds the fault within twenty minutes.

Two a.m., laptop at eleven percent battery, and the hostel's power had gone off at midnight. Pradeep's project was due at nine.
He had been changing lines at random since dinner. Nothing worked, and now he could not even remember which changes he had undone.
Rukmini, his lab partner, messaged: "Stop. Start a log. What you change, what happens."
He opened a blank note on the side of the screen. 2.04: removed the sort call, same crash. 2.09: printed the list length, it was zero. 2.11: checked the file path. Wrong folder.
There it was. The program had never been reading the file at all.
At 2.22, with four percent battery left, the program ran clean. Pradeep saved, plugged into Rukmini's power bank from across the corridor, and slept.

qa.q: What time did the program finally run clean?
qa.a: At 2.22, with four percent battery left, the program ran clean.

qa.q: How might Pradeep have felt when he found the wrong folder?
qa.a: He probably felt a rush of relief mixed with embarrassment, since hours of random edits had missed a simple wrong file path.

qa.q: What else could Pradeep do from the start of the next project?
qa.a: He could keep the change log from the very first bug, not only after hours of guessing, so each attempt teaches him something.

qa.q: How might Rukmini see that short message making such a difference?
qa.a: Rukmini may feel glad and a little proud that one clear suggestion turned a panicked night into a quick fix.

grounding: It shows a student who stops making random edits, keeps a log of each change and result, and finds the fault within twenty minutes.
